moves.spoken: We push d4 and offer the Scotch Gambit.
Black takes the pawn on d4.

We develop the bishop to c4 — this is the Scotch Gambit, a hybrid of the Scotch and the Italian. It's a genuinely dangerous, grandmaster-approved weapon, and a fine alternative if you like the Evans Gambit; at club level its traps bring quick wins.

Black plays d6, a solid, slightly passive choice that sidesteps the gambit's traps — a line playable with the black pieces too, leaving a marginally worse game. The point of the early bishop, as in the Italian, is access to the g5-square, where a knight or bishop is a key resource in many lines.

We recapture on d4 with the knight, regaining the gambit pawn and opening lines. White has the pleasant side — better central control, the bishop raking from c4 as in a good Scotch, and the sacrificed pawn already back.
Black develops the knight to f6. Should we fear a capture on d4 that drops the queen into the centre?

We develop the knight to c3. No — a capture on d4 wouldn't scare us: Black has no second knight on b8 to come to c6 and harass the queen, so it would just be well-placed for us to strike at. This is the same solid setup you can reach through a Philidor move order.
Black tucks the bishop to e7 — very solid, the d6-pawn restraining our e-pawn. Don't lunge at Black's throat here.
We castle. Rather than force matters, nurture the edge: complete development and enjoy White's space and well-placed pieces.

Black castles. Now a deceptively tricky moment. f4 is premature with the queen undeveloped, and the natural bishop moves to e3 or g5 each walk into tactics: after the bishop to e3, the knight to g4 is annoying, and worse, the shot on e4 — because ...d5 then regains the piece and forces the mass trades we're trying to avoid.
The move that permanently removes that idea is the bishop to b3: it drops the bishop onto a defended square, out of reach of a future ...d5 pawn fork.
An alternative was f3 — slightly weakening, but playable: it would let the bishop go to e3 and immediately cover the diagonal f3 opens.
Black's knight heads to e5 — an odd move that walks straight into a hit.
We don't need h3; we strike at once with f4, since Black's knight there isn't stable — we kick it and seize more of the centre.
f4 was dismissed a moment ago only because it came without tempo; now that the bishop sits safely on b3, the same break is better justified and safer.

Black plays the bishop to g4, hitting the queen — but that's all it does, and the bishop can land in real trouble. Where to put the queen? On a square where it also does something: d2 is awkward and d3 is covered by the knight, so the queen goes to e1 — from there it can later swing to g3, and it doesn't block our bishop. Simple logic is often the right logic.
The queen steps to e1, eyeing the later lift to g3 to x-ray the king.
Black reroutes the knight to d7.

We play h3, and the g4-bishop is in trouble. If it retreats to b6 we win the exchange — not with f5, which lets Black out, but by taking on e6: after the recapture, the knight lands on e6, forking king, queen and rook. If instead the bishop goes to h5, we trap it plainly: g4, the bishop drops to g6, and f5 corners it. Advancing a second pawn in front of the king is justified here because Black simply has no firepower near it, winning a piece is a big event, and the queen can always come to g3 to shelter our king.
Black gives up the bishop, taking on h3.
We recapture with the g-pawn — the pawn on h3 lends the king some shelter.

The way to have rescued the bishop was a counter-attack: ...c5, hitting the knight. If the knight moves, the bishop can grab it and then drop back to e6 — but this is panic, because with the trade the e6-square is no longer covered.

A key habit: after winning the bishop, don't submissively drop the knight back to f3 — see how the trade changed things. The f5-square has cleared, so the knight belongs there: every piece then points at Black's king, and on top of the extra piece we're building a powerful attacking machine.

Even better than the immediate queen to g3 (which Black meets with ...g6, biting on granite) is the central break e5 — opening a second front: we keep the g3 idea in our pocket while also striking down the middle, and the two threats together crush Black.
We open the centre with the capture on e5.
We recapture on e5, and Black's position is falling apart.
Black tries the knight to h5. No matter that the queen can't go to g3 now — we have a stronger idea.
We push e6, unleashing the b3-bishop's full potential: it's crushing, hitting the knight, the pawn, and the bishop, which all fall.

The finish is a lesson in undefended pieces. A "type-one" undefended piece is a hanging one, guarded by nothing; a "type-two" is guarded by only a single piece — and by prying open the e-file we exploit exactly that, since the queen is a poor defender. The clean win is e-takes-f7, but we can take the bishop first: if Black recaptures, then e-takes-f7 wins the queen — even ...Rxf7 leaves the rook pinned. Up two pieces, we then just consolidate. When the queen comes to b6 setting up an x-ray with a ...c4-check threat, the strongest reply isn't the passive block but the queen to e6, using the trade as a weapon: it forces the queen back, plants ours in Black's face, and clears the way for the bishop to e3. Purdy's rule holds — you play to win points, not to paint pictures; up material, resist the flashy move and take the simple win.
